content: Exclusive breastfeeding (EBF) for the first six months of life has been shown to reduce the risk of necrotizing enterocolitis in infants. Studies have not demonstrated any advantage of infant formula over EBF during this period. The Guideline Development Group (GDG) emphasized that EBF until six months is the standard of care for preterm and low birth weight (LBW) infants in many countries, forming the basis of numerous national policies and programs. Mothers should be encouraged and supported to provide their own breast milk, including colostrum, both before and after birth. The World Health Organization (WHO) defines EBF as feeding infants only breast milk, with no other foods or fluids (not even water), except for medicines, vitamins, and minerals. EBF is recommended for full-term, normal birth weight infants until six months of age. However, preterm and LBW infants are more vulnerable to nutritional deficiencies. Risks associated with contamination of complementary foods and early formula feeding are well-documented. In 2011, WHO recommended EBF for preterm and LBW infants until six months, but new studies have since emerged. Evidence on the effectiveness of EBF for six months versus less than six months was derived from two randomized controlled trials (RCTs) involving 307 preterm or LBW infants in Honduras and India. The trial in Honduras included 119 term small-for-gestational-age (SGA) infants who received nutrient-rich complementary foods starting at four months. The Indian study involved 403 infants born before 34 weeks of gestation, with complementary foods introduced at four months corrected age. Critical outcomes included morbidity (days with diarrhea or fever), growth (weight gain, length gain, and weight-for-age z-scores), and neurodevelopment (time to achieve motor milestones). No trials reported mortality. For growth outcomes, very low-certainty evidence from one trial with 119 participants suggested a decrease in weight gain from four to six months of age. Subgroup analyses on gestational age and birth weight could not be conducted due to insufficient trials. Families often express a desire to be actively involved in infant care, including decisions about feeding and nutrition. Challenges in providing breast milk after returning home include balancing work commitments, maternity leave, nighttime feeding, and partner support. Concerns about formula feeding include nutrient composition, water supply, contamination, and cost. Families value having formula available when circumstances require it, such as work commitments or insufficient breast milk supply. However, no specific evidence was found on whether families value EBF for six months for preterm or LBW infants. Promotion of EBF for six months should be integrated into community and facility-level care, extending through antenatal and postnatal periods. National or local guidance should address infrastructure, equipment, and supplies for healthcare facilities. Health workers at all levels can promote EBF, but standardized training, supervision, and monitoring are essential. Iron supplementation is recommended for preterm or LBW infants fed human milk who are not receiving iron from other sources. The GDG noted limited data on the dose, timing, and duration of supplementation. Based on most trials, a daily dose of 2–4 mg/kg of elemental iron may be initiated once enteral feeds are well-established and continued until the infant receives iron from another source. Iron deficiency is associated with poor growth and developmental outcomes in preterm and term infants. Human milk may not meet the iron needs of preterm or LBW infants due to low iron stores, red blood cell expansion, catch-up growth, and blood loss. Evidence suggests that enteral iron supplementation improves hematological outcomes but lacks sufficient data on growth and neurodevelopmental effects. Zinc supplementation may be considered for preterm or LBW infants fed human milk who are not receiving zinc from other sources. The GDG recommends a daily dose of 1–3 mg/kg of elemental zinc, initiated when enteral feeds are well-established. Zinc deficiency is linked to dysfunction in multiple physiological systems, including immune and skeletal systems. Human milk may not meet the zinc needs of preterm or LBW infants due to low zinc stores and catch-up growth. Evidence suggests zinc supplementation reduces mortality and improves short-term weight gain and linear growth, but its effects on common morbidities of prematurity are minimal. Vitamin D supplementation may also be considered for preterm or LBW infants fed human milk who are not receiving vitamin D from other sources. The GDG suggests a daily dose of 400–800 IU, initiated when enteral feeds are well-established. Vitamin D enhances calcium and phosphorus absorption and supports bone mineralization. Deficiency is associated with seizures, rickets, osteopenia, and increased risk of respiratory and diarrheal diseases. Human milk may not meet the vitamin D needs of preterm or LBW infants due to low stores and catch-up growth. Evidence indicates improvements in vitamin D biomarkers but limited data on other markers of bone health. Vitamin A supplementation may be considered for preterm or LBW infants who are not receiving vitamin A from other sources. The GDG suggests a daily dose of 1000–5000 IU, initiated when enteral feeds are well-established. Vitamin A supports cellular growth, mucosal integrity, and immune function. Preterm infants are born with low vitamin A stores, and supplementation has been shown to reduce bronchopulmonary dysplasia in very preterm infants. Evidence on the effects of vitamin A supplementation on mortality and morbidity is limited. In all cases, families need accurate information on the dose and administration of supplements. National or local guidance should be followed, and health workers should support families through standardized training and monitoring. Documentation of supplementation in clinical records is essential. However, evidence on the feasibility and equity of providing these supplements to preterm or LBW infants remains limited.
